Our local PBS Station did a rerun of Ken Burns's Civil War. One of the sources Mr. Burns used were quotations from a southern woman Mary Chestnut. Well I wanted to look up the quotations and see if there were any other writing of Mary Chestnut. I found out that the quotations are from the journals she kept during the Civil War. They have been published in a book called "Diary from Dixie" published in 1904.

The journals are interesting reading for a number of reasons. First of all Mary Chestnut was the wife of James Chestnut who was Jefferson Davis's chief of staff. In that position Mary moved among the highest circle of southern leadership, and had an insider's view of the the civil war from a confederate point of view.

How ever the most important thing from the Journals are when you read between the lines and compare it with human nature. In the social circle that Mary Chestnut traveled she would have been ostracized for any radical views of society. The fact that she and her husband were paying slaves a salary would have been looked down upon by others in her social circle had it not been some what common. There are also some passages about freeing slaves, (she and her husband wanted to do it, but her husbands father who held the property was against it.) Again while this view was not held by most of the southern aristocracy if must have been some what common.

The last thing that I find striking is while she writes about slaves and others in high social positions, but never mentions post masters, rail road workers, plant workers, store owners, small farmers, etc. who were the back bone of the confederate army. I have taken this position as meaning that the southern aristocracy didn't hold the average white worker as some one of value. In fact I think the members of the Southern aristocracy thought more of their slaves than the did of the railroad engineer who operated their trains that they road on.

Any way it is a book that any student of the civil war needs to read. (You can down load it from the University of South Carolina Chapel Hill archives)
